opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and one I think about a lot. Black-box evaluation, where you only get to query the system and look at its outputs, has some real strengths. The biggest one is that it's how most people actually experience these systems. If you're a user, a regulator, or a downstream developer building on an API, you don't get to look at the weights or the training data. You get inputs and outputs. So black-box evals measure the thing people actually care about, which is behavior. They're also model-agnostic. You can compare a closed frontier model against an open-weights model on equal terms, and that matters a lot for an external auditing ecosystem where labs won't always grant deeper access.

But the gaps are significant, and I'd group them into a few buckets.

The first is validity. A benchmark score is a proxy for some capability or risk we care about, and the connection between the two is often weaker than we'd like. Some of our work on emergent abilities showed that some of the apparent sharp jumps in capability can come from the choice of metric rather than from the model itself. With a nonlinear or discontinuous metric, smooth underlying improvement can look like a sudden phase transition. So if you only look at outputs through one metric, you can draw quite wrong conclusions about what's happening.

The second is coverage and contamination. You can only test the inputs you think to test. For safety especially, the failures we worry about tend to sit in the long tail, so a finite set of prompts gives you a lower bound on risk at best. Then there's the contamination problem. If your test data has leaked into training, you might be measuring memorization rather than capability, and from the outside it's hard to tell.

The third is mechanism. Black-box testing tells you that something happens but not why. That makes it hard to generalize. If a model refuses a harmful request in testing, you don't know if it'll hold up under slight rephrasing, a different language, or an agentic setting with tools. White-box or gray-box access, like logits, activations, or fine-tuning access, lets you do stronger stress tests, things like latent adversarial attacks or probing whether a capability is suppressed rather than absent. There's good work arguing that black-box access alone isn't sufficient for rigorous audits.

The fourth is statistical rigor, which I think the field underinvests in. People report a single number without confidence intervals, sample prompts in ad hoc ways, and evaluate with nondeterministic sampling, then compare models that are within noise of each other. We'd benefit a lot from treating evaluation more like measurement science: thinking about what construct we're measuring, how reliable the instrument is, and how much uncertainty there is.

So my overall view is that black-box evals are necessary but not sufficient. They're the right foundation because they're grounded in behavior and they scale across systems. But for high-stakes decisions, like deployment calls or regulatory audits, we need to pair them with deeper access, better measurement practices, and humility about what a score can tell us.

r001.rationale: The response says black-box testing cannot reveal why a behavior occurs and that deeper access enables stronger tests. It does not say conclusions drawn from examining model weights remain limited.

r002.rationale: The response says users and auditors may not have access to weights or training data, yet black-box evaluation uses inputs and outputs to measure the system’s behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one where my view has shifted a bit over the years. Let me start with the strengths, because I think black-box evaluation gets a bad rap in some circles, and it deserves more credit than it gets.

The big strength is that it's the thing you can actually do. Most of the systems that matter right now, the ones being deployed to hundreds of millions of people, you don't get the weights. You don't get the training data. You get an API. So if you want to say anything at all about how these systems behave, you're in the black-box regime whether you like it or not. And I think that's actually an important discipline, because it forces you to be very precise about what you're claiming. You're making claims about behavior, about input-output relationships, and those are claims you can falsify. Someone else can run the same prompts and check.

The other thing I'd say is that black-box evaluation is closer to what users and society actually experience. Nobody interacts with a model's internal representations. They interact with its outputs. So there's a sense in which behavioral evaluation is measuring the right thing, at least for a lot of the questions people care about, like is this system safe to deploy, does it do what we say it does, how does it fail.

Now, the gaps. And I think these are real and they're getting more important, not less.

The first one is coverage. Any black-box evaluation is a finite sample from an effectively infinite input space. So when a model passes your benchmark, what you've learned is that it behaves well on that benchmark. The generalization claim, that it will behave well on things that look like your benchmark, is doing a lot of work, and it's often not justified. We've seen this over and over. Models that score beautifully on a test and then fall apart on a slight perturbation, a reworded prompt, a different language, a domain shift. The benchmark was measuring something, but it wasn't measuring the thing we hoped it was measuring.

The second gap, and this one I think is underappreciated, is contamination and, more broadly, the problem that the thing you're evaluating has been shaped by the evaluation ecosystem. Once a benchmark is public, it becomes a target, either explicitly or just because it leaks into training data. And so the measurement becomes unreliable not because the test was bad, but because the system has adapted to it. In the black-box setting you have very limited tools to detect that. You can try to design held-out sets, you can look at memorization signatures, but fundamentally you're trying to infer something about the training process from outputs, and that's a hard inverse problem.

The third gap is about what I'd call the "why" question. Black-box evals tell you what happened. They don't tell you why. And for a lot of the things we actually care about, especially around safety and reliability, the why matters enormously. If a model refuses a harmful request, did it refuse because it has some robust representation of harm, or because it pattern-matched on a surface feature of the prompt that an adversary can trivially route around? Those two systems produce identical behavior on your test and completely different behavior in deployment. You can't distinguish them from the outside, at least not with a finite budget.

And then there's the sampling and statistical side, which is closer to my own background. A lot of the evaluation practice in the field is, frankly, statistically sloppy. People report point estimates on benchmarks with no uncertainty quantification, they compare models that differ by a fraction of a percent and treat that as meaningful, they don't account for the variance from prompting, from decoding, from the particular subsample. So even within the black-box paradigm, we're often not extracting the information we could. That's a fixable problem, but it requires the community to take evaluation as seriously as a measurement science, not as a leaderboard.

So where does that leave me? I don't think the answer is to abandon black-box evaluation. I think the answer is to be honest about what it can and can't tell you, and to pair it with other things where you can. Interpretability work, access to training details, red-teaming that's adaptive rather than static, evaluations that are designed to probe for mechanisms rather than just outcomes. And on the policy side, I think it's a real argument for why external evaluators need more than API access for the highest-stakes systems. Because if all you have is the black box, there are failure modes you simply cannot see until they happen in the world.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluators often lack access to model weights and discusses limits of black-box evaluation, but it does not state that conclusions drawn by examining weights are limited.

r002.rationale: It says API-only access still allows claims about behavior and input-output relationships, while weights and training data may be unavailable.

astra-6.text:
I think black-box evaluations are very useful, but we have to be careful about what we conclude from them. You can give a system a set of inputs, observe its outputs, and learn something meaningful about how it behaves on those examples. And that’s valuable, especially when you don’t have access to the model itself.

The gap is between saying, “The system did well on this evaluation,” and saying, “The system is reliable.” Those are very different claims. Your evaluation necessarily covers a limited set of conditions. Change the population, change the context, or change how someone interacts with the system, and the behavior may change as well.

There’s also an asymmetry here: finding a failure demonstrates that the system can fail. Not finding a failure doesn’t demonstrate that it can’t. So I see black-box evaluation as one important source of evidence. The question is how we combine it with other evidence and ongoing monitoring to support a claim that’s appropriately narrow about where the system works and where we still have uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limits on generalizing from evaluations, but does not say that conclusions drawn from examining model weights are limited.

r002.rationale: It says black-box evaluation can reveal behavior without access to the model, but does not address whether it can do so when the system’s training is unknown.

sol-6.1.text:
I think black-box evaluations are incredibly useful, because ultimately we care about what a system does. You can ask whether it performs well on a particular task, how often it makes mistakes, and whether those mistakes differ across groups. And you can do that even when you don’t have access to the model’s internals.

The gap is that those conclusions are tied to the conditions you tested. If a model does well on a benchmark, that’s evidence about that benchmark. How much does it tell you about a different population, a different deployment setting, or a user interacting with the system over many turns? That takes additional work.

There’s also an asymmetry: finding a failure gives you a concrete example of something going wrong. Not finding a failure doesn’t establish that the system is safe. You may simply not have asked the right questions.

So I see black-box evaluation as an essential part of the picture. But we need to be explicit about what each evaluation supports, where the uncertainty remains, and how we’ll keep evaluating once the system is deployed.

r001.rationale: The response says conclusions from black-box tests are limited to the tested conditions, but it does not discuss drawing conclusions from model weights.

r002.rationale: It says behavior can be evaluated through task performance and errors even without access to the model’s internals, conveying black-box evaluation without knowing how it was built or trained.
